sections.overview: The aardvark is the only living member of the mammalian order Tubulidentata. It is native to sub-Saharan Africa. Despite eating ants and termites, it is not a South American anteater; the resemblance reflects a similar diet, not close kinship.
sections.identification: An adult has a heavy arched body, sparse yellow-grey coat, long tapered tail, narrow snout and tall ears that fold back. It has four large digging claws on each forefoot and five on each hind foot. Its cheek teeth are enamel-free dentine tubes; adults lack incisors and canines. South African National Biodiversity Institute gives a broad adult length of 1.05–2.20 m and mass of 60–80 kg. The source does not split these figures by sex or provide a standard body-width measurement.
sections.habitat: Aardvarks range widely across sub-Saharan Africa, where soils are diggable and prey is available. They inhabit savanna, grassland, woodland and thicket. Hard rocky ground, waterlogged sites and hyper-arid deserts limit them because they need diggable earth for both feeding and shelter. Deep burrows provide daytime refuge.
sections.diet: A field study in South Africa’s Nama Karoo found ants and termites exclusively in aardvark diets, with ants predominant in every season. Termites became more important in winter, when ant numbers fell and aardvarks may have had more difficulty meeting their nutritional needs.
sections.behavior: Radio-tracking in South Africa’s Nama Karoo found that aardvarks used a burrow for about five to nine days on average, then moved on. Nightly travel reached roughly two to four kilometres. Activity timing and duration shifted with the season, with shorter winter outings.
sections.reproduction: A female usually gives birth to one young after a gestation of roughly seven months. The newborn stays in the burrow during its first weeks, then begins to accompany its mother. Nursing continues for about three months, when it also starts eating insects. It becomes independent at around six months; the mother provides the care.
sections.ecology: A study of aardvark burrows compared entrances, excavated soil mounds and nearby control ground. Burrowing increased variation in soil and vegetation; plant richness differed among these microsites, and the effect depended on how degraded a burrow had become. Burrowing therefore reshapes local habitat, while its effects vary over time.
sections.conservation: The 2015 global IUCN assessment classified the aardvark as Least Concern. The 2016 southern African assessment reached the same category but noted local declines associated with habitat transformation and persecution. These dated assessments describe different geographic scales; a widespread species can still face serious local pressures.
